newsitem.title: UK: Loyalists keep N.Ireland on truce tenterhooks.
newsitem.headline: Loyalists keep N.Ireland on truce tenterhooks.

text.p: Northern Ireland nervously waited on Sunday for any indications whether hardline Protestants would abide by a ceasefire they declared two years ago in their guerrilla struggle to remain a part of Britain.

Leaders of the outlawed Combined Loyalist Military Command, an umbrella group for pro-British Protestant guerrillas, met secretly on Friday but made no announcement on whether they would resume attacks on the province's pro-Irish Catholics.

Fears of retaliation by the so-called Loyalists mounted after the Catholic-based Irish Republican Army switched a bombing campaign from mainland Britain to the province, dealing a fresh blow to faltering peace efforts.

IRA fighters breached massive security at British military headquarters at Lisburn, south of Belfast, last Monday and detonated two 500 lb (225 kg) car bombs, killing a soldier and wounding 30 people.
Loyalist politicians linked to the Protestant guerrillas urged them to heed a yearning for peace and maintain the truce.

"Listen to what the people are saying," said Billy Hutchinson, a spokesman for the political wing of the banned Ulster Volunteer Force. "The people will tell us that there is no way that they want violence to return to the streets."

A Belfast newspaper predicted that the Loyalist military command would stick to its truce. Some Loyalist supporters said it might issue a statement on Sunday to mark the ceasefire's second anniversary but others said it might remain silent.

Security analysts said a protracted silence by the Loyalist command could be interpreted either as a de facto continuation of the truce or as a warning to the IRA that it could strike back if it chose.

Last Monday's IRA bombing was the first in Northern Ireland for two years. The IRA, which fought for 25 years to end British rule and unite with the Irish republic, ditched its own ceasefire last February and exploded bombs in British mainland cities.
Loyalist politicians argue that they would be expelled from Anglo-Irish sponsored multi-party peace talks, launched in June, if Protestant militants resumed attacks on Catholics.
They say the talks represent the only way forward for the province's Protestant majority and Catholic minority to work out a shared future.

The IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, excluded from the talks unless its guerrilla allies declare a new ceasefire, says the current round should be scrapped and replaced with unconditional negotiations.
